title: Keeping healthy: food, germs, moving and teeth
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Stage 2 Biology Unit 4.4 'Keeping healthy' (healthy eating, germs and being ill, exercise, keeping clean) and Unit 4.5 'Teeth' (types of teeth, looking after teeth, sugar and teeth). No textbook needed.
summary: Your child finds out that the food they eat becomes their body, so a varied plate matters; that germs are real living things too small to see, and that soap and water break them up; that exercise makes the heart, a muscle, stronger; and that we get only two sets of teeth in a whole life. They meet the friendly microbes that live inside us, the doctor who was laughed at for asking doctors to wash their hands, and the scientist who found out what really makes holes in teeth.
builds_on: This is the first rung of the health ladder. It links back to 'Living and non-living' (Class 1: living things feed, grow and get rid of waste). Class 3 adds hygiene of every outer organ, yoga, sleep and feelings; Class 4 adds medicines, vaccines and the journey of our food; Class 5 adds how diseases spread and how whole towns stop them.
goals: By the end your child can explain that what we eat becomes our body, and choose a plate with many kinds of food.
By the end your child can explain that germs are tiny living things, show how they spread, and wash hands properly with soap.
By the end your child can feel and count their own heartbeat before and after exercise, and say why the heart beats faster.
By the end your child can name incisors, canines and molars and say what each does, in humans and in other animals.
By the end your child can explain how sugar and mouth bacteria make holes in teeth, and why adult teeth must last a whole life.
subconcepts: food becomes our body (we are built from what we eat)
a varied diet: energy foods, body-building foods and protective foods
water: why the body needs it
germs are tiny living things (bacteria and viruses)
how germs spread: hands, sneezes, food and water
soap breaks germs' oily coats; washing for 20 seconds
most microbes are friendly: the microbes in our gut
exercise: muscles and the heart get stronger
heartbeat and breathing speed up when we move
rest and sleep let the body mend
milk teeth (20) and adult teeth (32): only two sets
incisors, canines and molars, and animals' teeth fit their food
plaque bacteria turn sugar into acid that dissolves enamel
brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste
words: diet
all the food and drink a living thing usually has
germs
tiny living things, too small to see, some of which can make us ill
bacteria
one kind of tiny living thing; most are harmless or helpful, some cause illness
microbe
any living thing too small to see without a microscope
exercise
using our muscles to move our bodies
heartbeat
the squeeze of the heart muscle that pushes blood around the body
incisors
sharp, flat front teeth for biting
canines
pointed teeth for gripping and tearing
molars
wide, bumpy back teeth for grinding
enamel
the hard white outer coat of a tooth, the hardest thing in the body
plaque
a sticky layer of bacteria that grows on teeth
fluoride
something added to toothpaste that makes enamel harder

days.title: You are made of your dinners
days.goal: Find out that food becomes our body, and hear the story.

steps.title: How did you get so big?
steps.do: Show your child a baby photo of themselves, or measure them against a door frame where you marked them last year. Ask: 'You were tiny once. Now you are big. Where did all the new you come from? What is your new arm made of?' Let them guess. Then say: 'Every bit of new you was built from food and water: the dal, the rice, the milk, the banana. The food you eat becomes your bones, your skin and your blood.' Ask: 'So if you ate only biscuits, what would your body have to build itself from?' (Only biscuits, which don't have the right building stuff.)

steps.title: What makes a healthy day?
steps.do: Ask your child to draw a quick picture or list of a healthy day from waking to sleeping. Then ask them to name 5 things that help a body stay well. Good answers: different kinds of food, clean water, washing hands, playing and running, sleeping, brushing teeth. Write their list on a sheet and stick it on the wall; this week you will test each one. Ask: 'Who keeps you healthy, apart from you?' (Family who cook, farmers who grow food, people who bring clean water, doctors, sweepers who clean the street.)

steps.title: Story: The Tooth Who Held the Door
steps.do: Read the story aloud (Story tab). Then ask the story questions. Don't explain the ending; let your child wonder about it.

steps.title: Wobbly tooth check
steps.do: Look in a mirror together. Your child counts their teeth, top and bottom, and wiggles each gently with a clean finger. Are any wobbly? Any gaps? Say: 'These are your milk teeth. Under them, your grown-up teeth are already waiting, like in the story.'

need: a baby photo or a door-frame mark

days.title: A plate with many colours
days.goal: Learn why we need many kinds of food, and water.

steps.title: What did you eat yesterday?
steps.do: Your child lists everything they ate and drank yesterday. Write it down. Ask: 'How many different colours of food were there?' Keep the list; you'll use it in Activity a1.

steps.title: Three jobs food does
steps.do: Explain with real foods on the table: 'Some foods are energy foods. They are like fuel for running and thinking: rice, roti, potato, poha, banana. Some are body-building foods. They help build muscles and mend cuts: dal, eggs, paneer, milk, chana, fish. Some are protective foods. They help keep you well and your eyes, skin and gums healthy: fruit and vegetables, like carrot, palak, amla, guava.' Ask: 'Which job does curd do?' (Body-building, and it also has friendly bacteria.) 'Can one food do everything?' (No, so we need many kinds.) Say: 'Sugar and oily snacks give quick energy but almost nothing to build with. They are a little-bit food.'

steps.title: Build a balanced thali
steps.do: Do Activity a1. Your child builds a thali from real food or drawings and checks it has food for all three jobs.

steps.title: Worksheet: food and germs (core), part A
steps.do: Do section A of Worksheet ws1 (food). Leave section B for Day 3. Ask your child to say why for each answer.

need: real foods from the kitchen or food pictures cut from packets

days.title: Germs: too small to see
days.goal: See how germs spread, and why soap works.

steps.title: Invisible living things
steps.do: Ask: 'Is there anything alive on your hands right now?' Say: 'Yes: millions of tiny living things called microbes. Most are harmless. A few kinds, called germs, can make us ill if they get inside us, through our mouth, nose or eyes.' Ask: 'How could a germ get from your hand into your mouth?' (Eating with unwashed hands, licking fingers, biting nails.)

steps.title: Haldi germs
steps.do: Do Experiment e1 with turmeric 'germs' and three kinds of washing.

steps.title: The doctor who said wash your hands
steps.do: Tell the story in voice v1 in your own words: about 180 years ago in Vienna, Dr Ignaz Semmelweis saw that mothers died more often in the ward where doctors worked. He made the doctors wash their hands, and far fewer mothers died. But many doctors were angry and would not believe him. Ask the voice question. Then finish Worksheet ws1 section B.

steps.title: Drama: the germ and the soap
steps.do: Act it out. One person is a germ, clinging to a hand (another person's arm) with an oily grip. The other is Soap: one hand grabs the oil, the other hand grabs Water, and together they pull the germ off and wash it away down the drain. Swap roles. Then ask: 'Why couldn't Water alone pull the germ off?' (Water slides off oil; soap holds on to both.) Children who act it remember the idea far better than ones who are told.

steps.title: Start the bread test
steps.do: Start Experiment e2: one slice of bread touched with unwashed hands, one with washed hands, one not touched. You will check it on Days 5, 6 and 7.

need: turmeric (haldi) and a few drops of cooking oil
3 slices of bread and 3 zip bags or steel tiffins with lids

prep.task: Buy a loaf of plain bread (no preservatives if possible)

days.title: Friendly microbes, and a muscle that never stops
days.goal: Meet the helpful microbes, and feel exercise working.

steps.title: The crowd inside you
steps.do: Say: 'Not all microbes are germs. Your gut, the long tube where food goes, has trillions of friendly bacteria living in it. They help break down food, make some vitamins and keep bad germs out by taking up the space.' Show a bowl of curd: 'Curd is milk changed by friendly bacteria. Idli and dosa batter rises because of friendly microbes too.' Ask: 'So are all germs bad? Are all microbes germs?' (No and no.) Ask: 'If you are full of bacteria, are you one living thing or a crowd?' Let them think; there's no single right answer.

steps.title: Heartbeat before and after
steps.do: Do Experiment e3: count heartbeats at rest, after one minute of jumping, and after two minutes of rest.

steps.title: Can you move just one toe?
steps.do: Try the DeepKids body challenge. Sitting still: move only your right big toe, nothing else. Now move only your right eyebrow. Now, without moving your head, look up towards the point between your eyebrows for 5 seconds. Then breathe out as slowly as you can and time it (breathing out slowly is safe; never hold the breath for long, and never in water). Ask: 'Was it easy to move just one part? Who was in charge of your toe?' Say: 'Your brain sends messages along nerves to each muscle. Practice makes the messages more exact.'

steps.title: Why the body needs rest and sleep
steps.do: Ask: 'After the jumping, what did your body want?' (To rest, breathe, drink water.) Say: 'Exercise makes muscles a little tired. While you rest and sleep, your body mends them and makes them a bit stronger than before. That's why children need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night.' Ask your child to count how many hours they slept last night (bedtime to waking). Ask: 'What happens to you the next day when you sleep too little?' (Grumpy, tired, can't think well.) Then sweat: 'Why do we sweat when we run?' (Sweat cools the skin as it dries. That is why we wash after exercise.)

need: a clock or phone timer with seconds

days.title: Biting, tearing, grinding
days.goal: Learn the three kinds of teeth and see how animals' teeth fit their food.

steps.title: Bread check
steps.do: Check the three bread bags from Experiment e2 without opening them. Any spots yet? Your child draws what they see in a table: Day, Touched dirty, Touched clean, Not touched.

steps.title: Three kinds of teeth
steps.do: With a mirror, your child finds: incisors (the flat, sharp front teeth, for biting), canines (the pointed ones at the corners, for gripping and tearing) and molars (the wide, bumpy back teeth, for grinding). Give a slice of apple, a piece of roti and a few roasted chana. Your child bites the apple (incisors), tears the roti (canines and incisors), crunches the chana (molars). Ask: 'Try grinding chana with only your front teeth. What happens?' (It's very hard: each tooth has a shape for its job.)

steps.title: Whose teeth are these?
steps.do: Show pictures (in a book or on a phone) of a cow's teeth, a tiger's teeth and an elephant's molar. Ask: 'Who eats grass? Who eats meat? How can you tell?' Good answers: the cow has wide flat grinding teeth for chewing grass all day; the tiger has huge canines for gripping and sharp back teeth for slicing meat. Tell them: 'An elephant grows six sets of big molars in its life, one after another. A shark keeps growing new teeth all its life. Humans get only two sets: milk teeth and adult teeth.' Ask: 'Which animal would you rather be, for teeth? Why?' Do Worksheet ws2 section A.

steps.title: Start the eggshell test
steps.do: Start Experiment e4: an egg in vinegar and an egg in water. Eggshell is made of much the same stuff as tooth enamel, so it shows what acid does.

need: an apple slice, a roti, roasted chana
pictures of cow, tiger and elephant teeth
2 raw eggs, 2 glasses, white vinegar, water

days.title: What really makes holes in teeth
days.goal: Find out how bacteria, sugar and acid make holes, and how brushing stops them.

steps.title: Eggshell results
steps.do: Look at the eggs from Experiment e4. Lift each out with a spoon. Ask: 'What happened to the shell in vinegar?' (It has bubbles, it went soft or disappeared.) 'In water?' (No change.) Say: 'Vinegar is an acid. And there is acid in your mouth too. Tiny bacteria in your mouth love sugar. When they eat it, they make acid, and the acid slowly eats into enamel, like the vinegar ate the shell.'

steps.title: The tooth worm that wasn't there
steps.do: Tell voice v2: for thousands of years, people in many countries believed a 'tooth worm' bored holes in teeth. In 1890, Willoughby Miller showed that the real cause was mouth bacteria making acid from sugar and starch. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Find the plaque
steps.do: Plaque is the sticky, almost invisible layer of bacteria on teeth. Before brushing tonight, your child runs their tongue over their teeth and feels the fuzzy coat. If you can get disclosing tablets from a chemist, chew one and look: the plaque turns pink. Otherwise eat a few jamuns or a beetroot slice and look in the mirror: the stain sticks to the plaque. Then brush for 2 full minutes (make up a brushing song together, one verse for top teeth and one for bottom, sung twice) with a pea-sized blob of fluoride toothpaste: small circles on the outsides, the insides, and back-and-forth on the chewing tops. Look again. Ask: 'Where was the plaque hiding?' (Near the gums and between teeth.)

steps.title: Datun: an old way
steps.do: Tell voice v3: in India, people have cleaned teeth with a neem or babool twig, chewed into a brush, for over two thousand years. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Worksheet: harder thinking
steps.do: Start Worksheet ws3 (challenge). Finish it tomorrow if needed. Also check the bread bags (e2) and add to the table.

need: disclosing tablets, or jamun or beetroot

days.title: Healthy body game and teach it back
days.goal: Put it all together and teach someone else.

steps.title: Bread verdict
steps.do: Open nothing; just look at the bread bags (e2) through the plastic. Which slice has the most mould? Ask: 'What does that tell you about our hands?' Then throw the bags away without opening them and wash hands.

steps.title: Healthy Body Race
steps.do: Play the board game g1 (print it). Talk about each square you land on.

steps.title: Project: my healthy-body book
steps.do: Finish the project: a little folded book with one page for each thing we found out (food, germs, soap, friendly microbes, heart, sleep, teeth, sugar). Your child draws and writes one sentence per page.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child teaches another family member how to wash hands properly and how to brush, and explains why. Then ask the check questions. Instead of labels like 'good boy' or 'clever girl', ask what they noticed and what surprised them; they are not their marks, and they can always look again.

need: the printed game board, a die, counters

sections.p: Sort these foods by their main job.
Why do we need many different kinds of food?
opts: because different foods give the body different things it needs

sections.p: The food we eat becomes our ____ .
Which drink does the body need most every day?
Your friend eats only chips for a week. What might happen to her body, and why?
Germs are…
opts: tiny living things too small to see
bits of dirt that are not alive

sections.p: Which of these spread germs?
Wash your hands with soap for at least ____ seconds.
In the haldi experiment, why did soap work better than water alone?
Match each tooth to its job.
A cow chews grass all day. Which teeth does it need most?
A tiger has very big…
Humans get only ____ sets of teeth in a whole life.
Sort the animals.
cats: gets many new sets of teeth

sections.p: Look at your own teeth. Do you have incisors, canines and molars? What does that tell you about what humans eat?
Your milk teeth will fall out. Does it matter if they get holes?
opts: yes: they hold the space for adult teeth and you need them to chew for years

sections.p: Why do you think an elephant needs six sets of molars, but a tiger doesn't?
What really makes holes in teeth?
opts: mouth bacteria making acid from sugar

sections.p: When is sugar worst for teeth?
opts: sipping a sweet drink slowly all afternoon

sections.p: The sticky layer of bacteria on teeth is called ____ .
The vinegar ate the eggshell. How is that like what happens in a mouth? How is it different?
Semmelweis told doctors to wash their hands. Why did many refuse?
opts: they couldn't see the germs and didn't like being told they caused harm
the mothers didn't want them to

sections.p: True or false?
items: curd is made by friendly bacteria
adult teeth grow back if they break

sections.p: Match the clue to the idea.
pairs: an old idea that turned out wrong
an old way to clean teeth

sections.p: How could you test whether the datun or a toothbrush cleans better? What would you need to keep the same?

experiments.title: Haldi germs
experiments.question: How do germs spread from hand to hand, and what really cleans them off?
need: a few drops of cooking oil
a bucket or tap of water
steps: Rub a few drops of oil over your child's palms, then sprinkle a pinch of haldi on and rub it in. Say: 'These are pretend germs. Germs on real hands stick in the skin's oils, just like this.'
Your child shakes your hand, touches a door handle, a spoon and a toy. Look at how the yellow has spread to everything.
Now wash one hand only with water for 5 seconds. Look.
Wash the other hand with soap for 20 seconds (sing 'Happy Birthday' twice): palms, backs, between the fingers, thumbs, and under the nails. Rinse. Compare the hands.
Wipe the door handle and spoon with soap and water too.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which will clean better: water alone, or soap? Will anything be left?'
experiments.observe: Water alone leaves most of the yellow; soap removes nearly all. The yellow hides longest between fingers, under nails and in skin creases.
experiments.why: Germs sit in the thin layer of oil on our skin, and water slides off oil. Soap is made of tiny particles with one end that grabs oil and one end that grabs water, so it lifts the oil and the germs away into the water. Soap can also break open the oily coat that some viruses wear, which destroys them. Haldi is only a pretend germ: real germs are far too small to see.
experiments.safety: Haldi stains clothes yellow, so wear old clothes. Keep it away from eyes.

experiments.title: The bread test
experiments.question: Do unwashed hands really carry living things?
need: 3 zip bags or tiffins with lids
steps: Label the bags 'dirty hands', 'clean hands' and 'not touched'.
Using tongs or the bag itself, put one slice straight into 'not touched' and seal it.
Before washing, your child rubs both hands all over the second slice. Seal it in 'dirty hands'.
Your child washes hands with soap for 20 seconds, dries them, and rubs the third slice. Seal it in 'clean hands'.
Keep all three in the same warm, dark place. Look on Days 5, 6 and 7 without opening the bags, and draw them.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which slice will grow spots first? Why?'
experiments.observe: Spots of mould, often green, black or white, appear first and most on the 'dirty hands' slice.
experiments.why: Mould is a fungus, a living thing. Its tiny spores were carried on unwashed hands, and some bacteria too. On warm, damp bread with food to eat, they grew until we could see them. Washing removed most of them. The untouched slice may still grow a little mould because spores float in the air everywhere.
experiments.safety: Never open the bags: mould spores can make people with asthma or allergies ill. Throw the sealed bags away at the end and wash hands.

experiments.title: Heartbeat before and after
experiments.question: What does exercise do to the heart?
steps: Your child sits still for 2 minutes. Find the pulse: two fingers on the inside of the wrist below the thumb, or a hand flat on the left of the chest. Count beats for 15 seconds; you can multiply by 4 later, or just compare 15-second counts.
Count breaths for 15 seconds too (watch the tummy rise).
Now jump, skip or run on the spot for 1 minute.
Count heartbeats and breaths for 15 seconds again. Feel the skin: warm? sweaty?
Rest for 2 minutes and count again.
Record all three in a table: Resting, Just after exercise, After resting.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will your heart beat faster, slower or the same after jumping? Why?'
experiments.observe: Heartbeat and breathing are much faster just after exercise and slow down again with rest.
experiments.why: Moving muscles need more oxygen and food. The heart is a muscle that pumps blood carrying oxygen and food to every part of the body, so when the leg muscles work hard, the heart pumps faster and you breathe faster to take in more oxygen. Exercising most days makes the heart muscle stronger, so it can push more blood with each beat.
experiments.safety: Stop if your child feels dizzy or unwell. A child with asthma or a heart condition should follow their doctor's advice.

experiments.title: What acid does to a shell
experiments.question: What can acid do to something hard like tooth enamel?
steps: Put one egg gently in a glass and cover it with vinegar.
Put the other in a glass of water.
Look after 10 minutes: tiny bubbles on the vinegar egg?
Leave both overnight, then lift them out with a spoon tomorrow and feel the shells.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'What will happen to each shell by tomorrow?'
experiments.observe: The vinegar egg fizzes and its shell becomes thin, soft or disappears, leaving a rubbery egg. The water egg doesn't change.
experiments.why: Eggshell is made mostly of calcium carbonate, a mineral. Acid dissolves it, giving off bubbles of a gas called carbon dioxide. Tooth enamel is a different calcium mineral, but acid dissolves it too, only more slowly. In the mouth, bacteria in plaque eat sugar and make acid right on the tooth. Every sugary snack gives them a fresh meal, and the acid can last about half an hour, so sipping sweet drinks all day is worse than having a sweet once. Saliva and fluoride help enamel repair tiny early damage.
experiments.safety: Don't eat the eggs afterwards. Wash hands after touching raw egg.

activities.title: Build a balanced thali
need: three small paper labels: energy, body-building, protective
steps: Put the three labels around the thali.
Your child picks foods to make one lunch and places each food near the label for its main job.
Check: is there at least one food for every job? Is half the thali vegetables and fruit?
Compare with yesterday's food list: which job was missing yesterday?
Ask: 'Who grew this food? Who cooked it?' Say thank you to them out loud.
activities.outcome: A thali your child designed, and a list of one change to try tomorrow.

project.title: My healthy-body book
steps: Fold 4 sheets of paper in half and staple them to make a small 8-page book.
Title it 'How my body stays well'.
One page each: what food does; germs and soap; friendly microbes; my heart and exercise; sleep; three kinds of teeth; sugar and acid; how to brush.
On each page, one drawing and one sentence in your child's own words.
Read it to a younger child, a cousin or a grandparent on a video call.
project.outcome: A small book your child wrote that explains how the body stays well, and why.

game.title: Healthy Body Race
rules: Print the board: 24 squares in a winding path.
Take turns to roll and move.
On a 'go' square, move forward the number shown; on a 'back' square, move back.
On a '?' square, another player asks a question from this week. A good answer with a reason lets you roll again.
First to HOME wins, but you must also explain one square you landed on.
squares: Ate dal, rice and sabzi: go 2
Played outside for an hour: go 2
Sipped a sweet drink all afternoon: back 3
Went to bed very late: back 2
Licked your fingers after the bus: back 2
Forgot to brush at night: back 2
Drank clean water after running: go 1

voices.who: Ignaz Semmelweis (1818–1865), Hungary, working in Vienna
voices.idea: In 1847 Semmelweis noticed that many more mothers died of fever after giving birth in the hospital ward where doctors and students worked than in the ward run by midwives. The doctors often came straight from cutting up dead bodies. He made them wash their hands in a chlorine solution before touching mothers, and deaths fell sharply.
voices.then: Many senior doctors rejected his idea. Germs had not yet been discovered, he could not explain why washing worked, and some were offended at the idea that their own hands caused deaths. He lost his job in Vienna.
voices.now: About twenty years after his death, Louis Pasteur, Robert Koch and others proved that germs cause many diseases. Semmelweis was right. Handwashing is now one of the most important ways to stop disease in every hospital. The midwives' ward had already shown the difference; their skill is often left out of the story.
voices.ask: Semmelweis had good numbers but couldn't explain why washing worked. Should doctors have tried it anyway? What would have convinced you?

voices.who: Willoughby D. Miller (1853–1907), American dentist working in Berlin
voices.idea: For thousands of years, people in Babylon, India, China and Europe believed that a 'tooth worm' made holes in teeth. In 1890 Miller published 'The Micro-organisms of the Human Mouth'. He showed that bacteria living on teeth turn sugars and starch into acid, and that the acid dissolves enamel.
voices.then: His idea was built on Pasteur and Koch's new germ science and was widely taken up by dentists.
voices.now: Scientists today agree that tooth decay is caused by acid from plaque bacteria (such as one called Streptococcus mutans) feeding on sugar, with diet, saliva and fluoride all playing a part. Nobody has ever found a tooth worm. Some people still think a hole is 'just bad luck'.
voices.ask: People believed in the tooth worm for thousands of years. Why do you think nobody checked? How could you check?

voices.who: Datun in the Sushruta Samhita (ancient India), and dentists today
voices.idea: The Sushruta Samhita, an ancient Indian book of medicine and surgery, describes cleaning the teeth every morning by chewing a fresh twig from bitter or astringent trees, such as neem, into a soft brush. People across India, Africa and the Middle East still use chewing sticks: neem, babool, and the miswak tree.
voices.then: For a long time, many European-trained doctors in India dismissed datun as old-fashioned.
voices.now: Some modern studies have found that a chewing stick used carefully can remove plaque about as well as a toothbrush, and neem has substances that slow some bacteria. But a twig carries no fluoride, which strongly protects enamel, and it is easy to use badly. Dentists today mostly recommend a brush with fluoride toothpaste; some say datun is fine as well. The question is still being studied.
voices.ask: How would you design a fair test of datun against a toothbrush? What would you measure?

story.title: The Tooth Who Held the Door
text: I am a milk tooth. I live in the bottom row of Meher's mouth, right at the front, between two other milk teeth called Left and Right. I have lived here for six years, which is the whole of my life and most of Meher's.

I came in when Meher was a baby. I remember the first thing I ever bit: a cold slice of cucumber from her Nani's kitchen in Lucknow. Meher dribbled and laughed and the whole family clapped, as if I had done something clever. I was very proud.

My job is biting. I am an incisor, flat and sharp. When Meher eats an apple, I go in first. When she eats a guava, I go in first. Behind me, at the back, live the molars, wide and bumpy, who do the grinding. The oldest molar is called Chakki, because he grinds like a flour mill. Chakki has a small brown hole in his top. He got it the year Meher's uncle came from Dubai with a whole suitcase of toffees, and Meher kept one in her cheek every afternoon for a month.

"The tiny ones did it," Chakki told me once. He meant the bacteria. Millions of them live in our mouth, too small to see. Most of them are quiet neighbours. But a few kinds love sugar more than anything, and when they eat it, they spit out acid. The acid is very small and very patient. It ate a door in Chakki's roof.
"Doesn't it hurt?" I asked.
"Sometimes," said Chakki. "When she drinks something cold."
This year, something strange started to happen to me. I began to feel a knocking underneath. Very slow, very gentle. Tap. Then nothing for days. Then tap again.

"Who's there?" I called down into the gum. Nobody answered. But the knocking went on, and slowly I began to feel loose. I wobbled when Meher ate. I wobbled when she talked. Meher started wiggling me with her tongue all day long, and I did not like it at all.
I asked Chakki what was happening. Chakki was quiet for a while.
"That," he said at last, "is the one who comes after you."
I didn't understand. I had thought I would be here for ever.

"Under every one of us," said Chakki, "there's a bigger tooth, growing in the dark. A grown-up tooth. It has been there for years, waiting. Now it's ready, and it's pushing up. As it pushes, your root is melting away to let it through. Soon you'll fall out, and it will take your place."
I felt very small then. Six years of biting cucumbers and apples and guavas, and now I was just going to be pushed out by someone I'd never even met.

That night Meher's mother looked in her mouth with a torch. "Wobbly!" she said. "Your first one." And then she said something I have thought about ever since. "Meher, the new tooth under there is a forever tooth. It has to last you seventy years, eighty, ninety. There's no third one coming after it. So we look after it."
No third one. I lay awake thinking about that, if a tooth can lie awake.

The new tooth would never be pushed out. It would bite Meher's apples when she was a teenager and a grown-up woman and a grandmother. Nothing would come up underneath to take its place. If the tiny ones ate a door in its roof, there would be no new tooth to fix it.

And then I understood what I had been doing all these years. I hadn't only been biting. I had been holding the place. If I had fallen out too early, the teeth beside me would have leaned into the gap, and the forever tooth would have come up crooked, or not had room to come up at all. Every year I stood here, I was keeping a door open for someone I had never met.
"Chakki," I whispered. "I was holding the door."
"We all are," said Chakki. "That's what milk teeth are for."
The knocking came again from below. Tap. This time I didn't mind it.
"Come up," I said to the one in the dark. "It's a good mouth. She likes apples. Watch out for toffees."

I fell out on a Tuesday, into a piece of roti. Meher held me up to the window and the light came right through me. Then she ran to show her mother, and her mother wrapped me in a twist of paper and put me in a little steel box.

From inside the box I can't see much. But the evenings now sound different. There is the sound of the tap running, and the scrub, scrub, scrub of the brush, and Meher's mother counting, "One minute… two minutes… done."

And down in the front of Meher's mouth, in the place I kept for six years, a small white edge is showing, with little bumps along its top like a new saw. It is bigger than I was. It looks surprised to be there.
Somebody held the door for it. It doesn't know that yet.
story.epiphany: We get only two sets of teeth: milk teeth hold the space and guide the adult teeth, which must last a lifetime because nothing replaces them. The turn is the milk tooth realising it was 'holding the door'. Chakki's brown hole quietly shows the other key idea: sugar-loving mouth bacteria make acid that eats into enamel. Underneath, there's something about doing your part for someone who comes after you.
ask: What was the knocking under the milk tooth?
Why did Meher's mother say the new tooth was a 'forever tooth'?
What does 'holding the door' mean for a milk tooth? What would happen if it fell out too early?
How did Chakki get his hole? Who are 'the tiny ones'?
Does anyone in your life hold the door for you?

ideas.idea: You are built from your food.
ideas.more: Every new bit of a growing child, from bones to blood, is made of what they eat and drink. Mark your child's height on a door frame each birthday: all that growth was dal, rice, milk and vegetables, turned into a person.

ideas.idea: You are never alone: you are a walking city of microbes.
ideas.more: Trillions of bacteria live in and on each of us, roughly as many as our own cells. Most help us. Germs are only a few troublesome kinds. Curd, idli and dosa are made by friendly microbes.

ideas.idea: Some things in your body are replaced, and some are not.
ideas.more: Skin, blood and hair are always being remade. Adult teeth are not: enamel can't grow back once it's lost. So caring for something that can't be replaced matters most.

unknowns: Exactly which of the trillions of microbes in our gut help us, and how, is still being worked out. Scientists find new kinds every year.
Why do some people get many holes in their teeth and others, eating the same food, hardly any? Saliva, genes and the mix of mouth bacteria all seem to matter, but nobody can fully predict it.

Could we one day grow a third set of teeth? Scientists are studying the genes that stop human teeth after two sets; some animals, like sharks and crocodiles, replace teeth all their lives. Nobody can do it in humans yet.
big: If you're made of the food you eat, were you once a field of rice?
Are you one living thing, or a crowd of living things?
Is a 'germ' bad, or just doing what it needs to live?
Why might people not believe something true when they can't see it?
Should every child in the world be able to get clean water and soap? Who decides?

challenge.q: 'All bacteria are bad and we should kill them all.' True?
challenge.hint: No. Most bacteria are harmless, and many are vital: they make curd, help digest food, make soil, and keep harmful germs out. Washing hands removes germs we pick up from outside; it doesn't empty us of our friendly microbes. Ask: what would happen if every bacterium on Earth vanished?

challenge.q: 'Milk teeth don't matter because they fall out anyway.'
challenge.hint: Dentists disagree. Milk teeth are used for chewing and talking for years, they hold the space for adult teeth, and a bad hole can hurt and spread infection. Ask: what would you say to a younger cousin who believes this?

challenge.q: 'Sugar makes children hyper.' Lots of parents believe it. Is it true?
challenge.hint: When scientists tested it carefully, giving some children sugar and some a sugar-free drink without telling anyone which was which, most studies found no difference in behaviour, but parents who thought their child had had sugar rated them as more hyper. Sugar is still bad for teeth. Ask: why might parents see something that isn't there?

perspectives.who: Your skin and your immune system
perspectives.view: Every living cell, from the very first ones billions of years ago, has had a skin of sorts, a membrane that keeps 'me' in and 'not me' out. Your skin and your germ-fighting cells still do that job. Ask: where do 'you' stop and the world begin, if the food on your plate becomes you tomorrow?

A cow chews for up to eight hours a day with wide, flat molars and no top front teeth at all, just a hard pad. Her stomach is full of microbes that digest grass for her. Ask: who does the cow's digesting, really?

perspectives.who: The safai karamchari (sanitation worker) who cleans your street
perspectives.view: Before doctors and medicines, the biggest drop in disease in many cities came from clean water, drains and taking away waste. The people who do this work keep a whole town healthy, often for little pay and little thanks. Ask: who keeps you healthy that you never see?

They live in the dark, eat what you can't digest and make some vitamins for you. If they could talk, what would they ask you to eat more of? (Scientists think they like fibre: vegetables, fruit, whole grains and dal.)

books.title: The Tooth Book
books.author: Theo. LeSieg (Dr. Seuss)
books.why: A rhyming book about who has teeth, who doesn't, and how to keep yours.

books.title: Germs Make Me Sick!
books.author: Melvin Berger
books.why: A clear first book on bacteria and viruses and how the body fights them.

books.title: Hear Your Heart
books.author: Paul Showers
books.why: How the heart works and how to listen to it, from the 'Let's-Read-and-Find-Out Science' series.

books.title: Tiny Creatures: The World of Microbes
books.author: Nicola Davies
books.why: Shows how many microbes there are and how much good they do.

check.q: Why do we need to eat many different kinds of food?
check.a: Different foods do different jobs: energy, building the body, keeping us well. Our body is built from what we eat.

check.q: What are germs, and how do they get into our bodies?
check.a: Tiny living things too small to see; through the mouth, nose and eyes, from hands, sneezes, dirty food and water.

check.q: Why does soap clean better than water alone?
check.a: Germs stick in skin oil; soap grabs the oil and lifts it and the germs away into the water.

check.q: What happened to your heartbeat after jumping, and why?
check.a: It got faster, because working muscles need more oxygen and food, which the blood brings.

check.q: Name the three kinds of teeth and their jobs.
check.a: Incisors bite, canines grip and tear, molars grind.

check.q: How do sugar and bacteria make holes in teeth?
check.a: Plaque bacteria eat sugar and make acid, which dissolves enamel.

check.q: Why must we look after adult teeth so carefully?
check.a: We get only two sets; adult teeth must last a lifetime and won't be replaced.
